title: Schedule a Conversation Instead of a Meeting
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author argues organizations hold too many meetings and too few conversations. Meetings, driven by status and agenda, invite competition for airtime, interruptions and digressions, while conversations are driven by questions and answers and emphasize understanding over advocacy. People show more genuine interest and open-mindedness in conversation. The obstacle is group size: conversations work only with a handful of people, about six at most, so meetings win by default as leaders invite everyone to be inclusive. The author concedes meetings have a place for information transfer and decisions. The practical suggestion is to limit the group and schedule a conversation when the goal is to explore an issue, strengthening relationships along the way.
points: Meetings tend to produce competitive airtime-seeking, while conversations produce mutual understanding.
Group size is the real constraint, since a conversation cannot sustain more than about six people.
Leaders over-invite in the name of inclusion, which lowers the quality of exchange.
Meetings remain right for information transfer and decision-making, but exploration is better served by small conversations.
quotes: In meetings, people often compete to stand out, get heard, and advocate for their ideas, resulting in unfocused discussions replete with interruptions and digressions. It's no wonder then that people don’t look forward to meetings and no one asks for more of them. Heaven forbid.
In contrast, conversations flow more naturally and leave everyone feeling heard and appreciated. Conversations are driven by questions and answers, not time-constrained topics on an agenda.

Because conversations are focused on exploring an issue, people show more genuine interest in what others think and remain open-minded. The mutual exchange of ideas, beliefs, and feelings places the emphasis on understanding and not on advocacy. People get a lot more done enjoyably through conversation.
Conversations can only happen with a handful of people. More than 6 team members can’t have a conversation. That’s why meetings trump conversations in most organizations.

Yet, the presumption that every issue, topic, and problem requires a herd of people isn’t always sound. In too many cases, leaders invite just about everyone to a meeting in an attempt to include, involve, and engage more people. The quality of the exchange suffers as a result.

Meetings certainly have their place. When designed correctly, they offer an efficient transfer of information and an effective forum for decision-making. But, more often than not, leaders would find more value in exploring an issue by limiting the number of team members and having a conversation instead.

More conversations and fewer meetings can make a big difference in how leaders and team members relate to each other. The electrical currents in good conversations meld people together. Meetings don’t have that juice.
